open-question.question: The extension contributes two commands today: `gurita.openMissionPane` (Gurita: Open Mission Pane), its only entry point, and `gurita.refreshMissionPane`. Once the activity-bar view is the entry point and the one mission pane no longer exists, which commands does the extension offer in the Command Palette, and do the two existing ones stay, change, or go?
open-question.recommendation: Both old ids name a pane that no longer exists, and at version 0.1.0, installed by hand, no binding is worth a permanent misnomer; refresh is the one action worth running without the side bar in view, since git state is not watched, and every other action stays in the entry point the goal names, one click away once the generated focus command shows the view.
open-question.alternative: The two existing command ids are removed, and the Command Palette offers one command of the extension's own beside the focus command VS Code generates for the view: a refresh command under a new id and a title naming missions rather than the pane (such as Gurita: Refresh Missions), re-reading the side-bar tree and every open mission and Settings window exactly as the side-bar's Refresh control does, the same registered command serving that control. The commands behind New mission, Define mission, Settings, and opening a mission are hidden from the Command Palette through `menus.commandPalette` entries whose `when` is `false`. The one action a person may want without looking at the side bar, re-reading after a change the watcher does not see (git state is not watched), keeps a palette entry, while every other action stays in the one entry point the goal names. The refresh command is renamed, so a keybinding bound to `gurita.refreshMissionPane` breaks, and Settings and individual missions still have no keyboard path by name.

The extension contributes no Command Palette command of its own. Both `gurita.openMissionPane` and `gurita.refreshMissionPane` are removed from the manifest and from `src/extension.ts`, and the side-bar view is reached from the Command Palette only through the focus command VS Code generates for every contributed view. The commands behind the side-bar's controls and its mission rows (Refresh, New mission, Define mission, Settings, opening a mission) are still registered, as tree items and view-title buttons need them, but each is hidden from the Command Palette through a `menus.commandPalette` entry whose `when` is `false`. The activity-bar view is the one entry point in fact as well as in name: the Command Palette adds no second way into anything, no command title exists that could drift from the control it duplicates, and the manifest and the stubbed tests lose both commands outright. Nothing the side bar does can be run from the keyboard by name, refreshing included, and any keybinding a person bound to either existing command id stops working with no replacement id to rebind.

Both existing command ids stay in the manifest and in the Command Palette with new titles and new behaviour: `gurita.openMissionPane` reveals and focuses the activity-bar view (titled, say, Gurita: Show Missions), and `gurita.refreshMissionPane` re-reads the side-bar tree and every open window (titled, say, Gurita: Refresh Missions) and backs the side-bar's Refresh control. No further command is added to the Command Palette, and the commands behind New mission, Define mission, Settings, and opening a mission are hidden from it. Every keybinding, task, or other extension already invoking either id keeps working, and the change of entry point costs a person who used the palette nothing to relearn. Both ids keep naming a mission pane that no longer exists, a permanent misnomer in the manifest, the code, and any documentation that cites the id, carried to protect the bindings of an extension at version 0.1.0 whose only entry point was this one command.

The two existing ids are removed, and the Command Palette offers, beside the focus command VS Code generates for the view, a refresh command under a new id, an Open Settings command opening (or revealing) the Settings window, and an Open Mission command that shows a quick pick of the live missions, each item the mission's title with its path, and opens (or reveals) the chosen mission's window. Each is the same registered command the matching side-bar control or mission row runs. New mission and Define mission are not offered in the Command Palette and stay side-bar controls only. Every window the mission opens up can be reached from the keyboard by name without the side bar, while the two run-starting controls, whose meaning depends on the variant shown beside them, are not split into a second form that shows no variant. The extension gains two commands and a quick pick to build and test against a `vscode` stub that stands in for no quick pick today, every palette title is a second label to keep in step with its control, and the old ids' keybindings break.

The two existing ids are removed, and every action the side-bar view carries is also a Command Palette command under a new id: a refresh command, Open Settings, Open Mission with a quick pick of the live missions, New mission, and Define mission, the last two asking their typed values in VS Code's input box as the side-bar controls do and running the variant those controls currently select (the remembered per-project selection under `gurita.projectVariantSelections`). Each palette command is the same registered command its side-bar control runs, so none is hidden from the Command Palette. Everything the extension does outside one mission's page can be done keyboard-only and bound to a key, and no registered command needs a `menus.commandPalette` entry to hide it. New mission and Define mission run from the palette without showing which harness, model, and effort they will use, so a person can start a run on a variant they did not see; how those controls show and select a variant is the sibling question Side-bar controls and variants, and this option holds only if its answer leaves a remembered selection a palette command can read. It is also the largest command surface to build, document, and test, and the old ids' keybindings break.

open-question.question: Today the extension reads the live missions and watches the mission files only while the mission pane exists, and while the pane is hidden a file event only marks it stale until it is shown again. With a side-bar tree listing every live mission and several mission windows open at once, from when until when does the extension read the missions and watch their files, and is a hidden side-bar view or a hidden window re-read on a file event or only once it is shown again?

alternative.id: First open to session end, eager

open-question.alternative: Start: nothing is read or watched until the side-bar view is first resolved (its first `getChildren` call, the view's own activation) or a Gurita command first runs. End: from then the live read and the one watcher last until the extension deactivates, never released when the view is hidden or every mission window is closed. Hidden surfaces: every debounced burst re-reads what it touches whatever is visible, the tree kept current while hidden and each hidden mission window drawing from the current read when it is shown and redrawn from its ready message. No stale flag exists. Nothing is spent until a person opens Gurita, and after that one lifecycle with no visibility tracking keeps every surface current, so the stale flag and the show-time catch-up read of today's pane are dropped rather than multiplied across the tree and several windows. Once opened, a side-bar view the person has switched away from keeps paying for every burst of a run's writes for the rest of the session, each burst that moves the live list re-running `missions.py live`, and since the editor restores a side-bar container that was open at the last close, in practice this often starts at startup anyway.

Start: the extension activates when a window opens on a workspace holding a mission (a `workspaceContains` activation event on the discovery pattern, beside the view's own activation), and at once runs `missions.py live`, reads every live mission's documents, and creates the one `FileSystemWatcher`. End: the watcher and the read last until the extension deactivates with the window, whatever is shown or hidden. Hidden surfaces: every debounced burst re-reads what it touches whether or not the side-bar view or any mission window is visible, so the tree is current while hidden, and a hidden mission window, which with `retainContextWhenHidden` off is redrawn from its ready message anyway, draws from that current read when shown. No stale flag exists. The side-bar tree, and anything drawn on the activity-bar entry itself such as the `TreeView`'s numeric badge, is current from the first moment of the session, before the person has opened Gurita at all, and showing any surface never waits on a read. Every session of every workspace holding a mission pays for a `missions.py live` subprocess, a read of every mission's documents, and a watcher, even when Gurita is never opened, and it departs from the first version's recorded rule that the extension activates on its command alone, adding an activation event the extension has never had.

alternative.id: First open to session end, stale until shown

open-question.alternative: Start: as with the eager first-open option, the first resolution of the side-bar view or the first Gurita command. End: the watcher lasts until the extension deactivates. Hidden surfaces: today's rule extended to each surface, a burst re-reading only for the surfaces visible at the time, while it marks the hidden side-bar view (told by the `TreeView`'s visibility change) and each hidden mission window (told by its panel's view-state change) stale, each stale surface re-read when it is next shown. It keeps the refresh behaviour the extension already has and its tests already cover, only applied per surface, and a hidden surface costs no read however many bursts a run writes. A stale flag and a show-time read must be kept for the tree and for every open window, which is the module-level state the starting state says nothing addresses apart from the one panel, and a surface shown after a burst briefly draws its old read; nothing on the activity-bar entry can be kept current while the view is hidden.

alternative.id: Only while visible, stale when hidden

open-question.alternative: Start: whenever at least one surface becomes visible, the side-bar view or a mission window, the extension reads the live missions afresh and creates the watcher. End: when the last visible surface is hidden, the watcher is disposed and its pending batch dropped, as today's pane disposes them with the panel. Hidden surfaces: while another surface is visible, a burst re-reads only for the visible ones and marks the hidden ones stale for a read when shown; while none is visible no event is seen at all, and the next surface shown starts with a full re-read. It carries today's rule, that with no pane open the extension reads no mission and watches no file, over to the new surfaces exactly, so Gurita costs nothing at all whenever it is out of sight. Every return after a hidden spell re-runs `missions.py live` and every mission's documents before the tree is current, switching side-bar containers creates and disposes a watcher each time, and it is the most involved lifecycle of the set, tracking visibility across the tree and every window at once.

alternative.id: Only while visible, eager when hidden

open-question.alternative: Start and end: as in the visibility-gated stale option, the read and the watcher begin whenever a first surface becomes visible and are released when the last one is hidden, a full re-read opening each visible spell. Hidden surfaces: while any surface is visible, every burst re-reads what it touches for all surfaces alike, so a hidden side-bar view stays current while a mission window is in front, and a hidden mission window draws from the current read when shown; only while nothing is visible is nothing read. It keeps the zero cost while Gurita is entirely out of sight but needs no per-surface stale flag, only one count of visible surfaces, so the tree is already current when the person switches back to it from a mission window. While one mission window is in front, a run going on another mission makes every burst re-read missions no visible surface shows, and each return after a fully hidden spell still pays the full re-read and the watcher churn of the visibility-gated design.

Start and end: no `FileSystemWatcher` exists at any time. Each surface reads when it is shown, the side-bar view when it becomes visible and a mission window when it is opened or shown, and everything is re-read at a run's end, as the `ended` listener does today, and by the Refresh control; file events are never seen, hidden or not. It removes the watcher, its debounce queue, and every stale flag outright, so there is no lifetime to manage and nothing to keep in step across the tree and several windows. A visible surface no longer follows a run's progress, each answer or task commit showing only at the run's end, and a hand edit, a run in an outside terminal, or a branch switch stays invisible until the person presses Refresh or hides and shows the surface, a regression from the live refresh the extension has today.

open-question.question: The harness check runs the first time the settings view is opened after the mission pane's panel is created, and its result is kept for that panel's lifetime and run again only by the check-again control. Once Settings is a window of its own and no single mission pane exists, when does the check first run, and for how long is its result kept before it runs again by itself?
open-question.alternative: The check first runs on the first opening of the Settings window after the extension activates, and its result is kept in the extension's own module state for the rest of that extension session, surviving every close and reopen of the Settings window; only the check-again control runs it afresh, and a restart or window reload, which ends the session, means the next first opening runs it again. The check runs at most once per session unless asked for, so reopening Settings is instant and shows the result at once, while a person who never opens Settings never pays for a run, keeping the check lazy as it is today. A result can grow stale for a whole session without sign: a harness CLI or Gurita copy installed or upgraded in a terminal after the first opening stays reported as missing or old until the person thinks to press check-again, and the result outlives any change of the project root it was run from.

The check first runs when the Settings window is created, from the side-bar view or from any mission window, and its result is kept in that window's state for as long as that window stays open: revealing the open window again, or its page redrawing after being hidden, posts the kept result without running the check. Closing the Settings window discards the result, so the next Settings window created runs the check again by itself. Between those, only the check-again control runs it afresh. It is the direct transposition of today's rule, with the Settings window standing where the mission pane's panel stood, so the recorded first-version behaviour and the settings view's code (state cleared on dispose, the first opening running the check) carry over with the least change, and a person who installs a Gurita copy in a terminal sees it the next time they open Settings after closing it. Settings is now a small window opened and closed often, so each reopening pays the check's run again (a login-shell session that looks up and lists all three harness CLIs, seconds rather than milliseconds) and shows it as running, where today the result survived as long as the one pane did.

The check first runs by itself when the extension activates (in effect when the side-bar view is first shown), before Settings is ever opened, and its result is kept in the extension's module state for that extension session, surviving every close and reopen of the Settings window; only the check-again control runs it afresh, and a restart or reload runs it again at the next activation. The result is usually ready the first time Settings is opened, so the person never waits on a running check there, and a session always opens with a current reading. Every session pays for a run that spawns a login shell and three CLI listings whether or not Settings is ever opened, its result reaching the settings view alone and changing nothing the side-bar or the mission windows draw or allow, and the stale-within-session cost of keeping one result for the whole session remains.

The check first runs on the first opening of the Settings window after the extension activates, and its result is kept in the extension's module state across closes and reopens of the Settings window, but an opening that finds the kept result older than a fixed age (on the order of minutes) runs the check again by itself, the kept result shown meanwhile; the check-again control still runs it afresh at any time, and a restart or reload discards the result. Reopening Settings soon after is instant, while a reopening after a while, the likely moment after a person has installed or upgraded a harness or its Gurita copy elsewhere, picks up the change without anyone pressing check-again. It adds a timing rule and a timestamp to state and to the tests, and a fixed age is arbitrary: an install made just before a reopening inside the window is still missed, and a long-lived window opened after the age passes shows a result that is replaced while it is read.

No result is kept between openings: the check runs by itself every time Settings is opened, whether the control creates the Settings window or reveals one already open, and the result is held only for drawing that window, a redraw after it was hidden posting what it holds; the check-again control still runs it afresh while the window is shown. What Settings shows is always as current as its last opening, so an install done anywhere is reflected the next time the person opens Settings, with no staleness rule to explain or test. Every opening shows the check as running and pays its seconds-long run, the check-again control becomes nearly redundant, and a person who opens Settings only to edit a variant waits on, or watches flicker, a check they did not ask for.

The check first runs on the first opening of the Settings window in a project that holds no stored result, and its result is stored in the extension's `workspaceState` (per project, since Claude Code's installed copy is chosen by the project root), so it survives closing Settings, restarts, and reloads; nothing runs it again by itself, only the check-again control, whose result replaces the stored one. The check is paid once per project and every later opening, in any session, shows a result at once, with the fewest runs of any option that still runs one without being asked. A stored result can be stale for days, across CLI and plugin upgrades, with only its stored date to warn of it, and it adds a stored record of the check that today's design deliberately kept in memory only, a staleness that a person relying on the view to see whether a harness is installed may not suspect.

The latest result is stored in the extension's `workspaceState` and shown at once when Settings is opened, marked as from an earlier check, while the first opening of Settings in each extension session also runs the check by itself; its fresh result replaces the shown one and the store and is then kept for the rest of the session across closes and reopens of the Settings window, the check-again control running it afresh at any time. Settings never opens blank or merely running, since the last known result is there at once, yet each session still refreshes it once without being asked, joining the instant display of a stored result to the per-session freshness of a session result. It is the most state of any option, a stored record beside a session copy and a marker telling an earlier result from a fresh one, all of which the pane tests' stub of `workspaceState` and the settings view's drawing must cover, and the shown result can briefly mislead before the fresh one lands.

The check never runs by itself: Settings opens with no result and a control (today's check-again, then its only trigger) that runs it, and the result is kept in the extension's module state for the rest of the extension session, across closes and reopens of the Settings window, until that control runs it again; a restart or reload discards it. No run is ever paid unless the person asks for it, and the check, whose result gates nothing the side-bar or the mission windows do, becomes an explicit diagnostic rather than a cost hidden in opening Settings. It reverses the recorded first-version behaviour of checking on first opening, and a person who opens Settings to see whether a harness is installed must notice and press a control first, so the view often shows nothing about the harnesses at all.

open-question.question: The banner's SVG is a tracked file regenerated by hand with `scripts/render_banner.py`, a stdlib-only Python script, and pinned to that script's output by `tests/test_banner.py`. The extension's other generated files are written into the git-ignored `gurita-vscode/bundled/` by the Node script `gurita-vscode/scripts/bundle.js` at every package. Where does the script that generates the activity-bar icon live and in which language, is the icon it writes a tracked file or a package-time output, and does a test pin the icon to the script's output?

alternative.id: Python sibling script, tracked, pytest pin

open-question.alternative: A new stdlib-only Python script beside the banner renderer at the repository root, `scripts/render_icon.py`, run by hand like `scripts/render_banner.py` and leaving that script unchanged. It reads `assets/banner.txt` and writes the icon as a tracked SVG inside the extension's own directory (for example `gurita-vscode/media/`), where the manifest's `viewsContainers` entry can name it and the VSIX carries it, since `assets/` lies outside the packaged root. A new pytest test under `tests/`, shaped like `tests/test_banner.py`, loads the script and asserts that the tracked icon is well-formed SVG and equals what the script renders from the drawing, so CI's two pytest runs catch a stale icon. It repeats a pipeline the project already runs and tests: the banner's recorded decision (a plain-text drawing as the source of truth and an SVG generated by a script run by hand) carries over unchanged, the icon is in every checkout with no build step, and the pin runs in CI, which runs pytest but no Node tests. The icon becomes a second derived file someone must remember to regenerate after any change to the drawing, caught only by a failing test, and a script outside `gurita-vscode/` produces a file inside it, so the extension's directory no longer holds everything that builds it, and the change needs CLAUDE.md's repository layout and the render-banner command line updated.

alternative.id: Folded into render_banner.py, tracked, pinned in test_banner

open-question.alternative: The icon is produced by `scripts/render_banner.py` itself, the stdlib-only Python renderer, so one run by hand writes both `assets/banner.svg` and the tracked icon inside `gurita-vscode/` (for example `gurita-vscode/media/`), reusing its drawing and colour-mask parsing. `tests/test_banner.py` is extended to assert that the tracked icon is well-formed SVG and equals the script's output, so the existing CI pytest runs pin both files. A drawing edit followed by the one documented command regenerates the banner and the icon together, so the two can never drift apart in a checkout, and the parsing of `banner.txt` stays in one place under one test file. It changes the contract of a finished mission's tool, which today takes any drawing path and writes only `<stem>.svg` beside it, by giving it a fixed second output in another directory. Its fit also depends on the axis the icon-mark-form question owns: an icon drawn in a form other than the banner's monospace text would put two unrelated renderers in one file.

A stdlib-only Python script under the repository's `scripts/`, run by hand, writes the icon as a tracked SVG inside `gurita-vscode/` for the manifest to name, and no test compares the tracked icon with the script's output. It is the least machinery: one script and one committed file, with no new test, no package-time step, and nothing for CI to keep green, which suits an icon that changes only when the drawing does. Nothing catches a drawing edit or a hand edit of the icon that was not regenerated, so the icon can silently stop being the script's output, unlike the banner, which the project chose to pin.

alternative.id: Node in bundle.js, package-time, no pin

open-question.alternative: The icon is generated in Node by the extension's own build step, `gurita-vscode/scripts/bundle.js` (or a sibling script it calls), which already reads files from the repository root at every package. It reads `assets/banner.txt` and writes the icon into the git-ignored `gurita-vscode/bundled/`, and the manifest's `viewsContainers` entry names `bundled/` for it. No icon file is tracked, so no test pins one; the package build failing is the generator's only check. The icon cannot go stale: it is rendered from the drawing at every `vsce package`, exactly as `bundled/` already carries the missions tool, the snippet file, the fixed lines, and the plugin version, so the extension's directory holds everything that builds it and nothing derived is committed. A checkout shows no icon in an Extension Development Host until `bundle.js` has been run, the manifest names a file that is not in the tree, the banner's drawing parsing is written a second time in another language, and the generator has no test, while CI runs no Node code at all.

alternative.id: Node in bundle.js, package-time, node:test of generator

open-question.alternative: The same package-time pipeline as rendering in `bundle.js`: Node code under `gurita-vscode/scripts/` writes the icon from `assets/banner.txt` into the git-ignored `gurita-vscode/bundled/` at every package, and the manifest names it there. In addition, a `node:test` test under `gurita-vscode/src/test/` runs the generator on the drawing and checks its output's shape (well-formed SVG, one fill colour, a 24-unit square view box, three arms), run by `npm test`. It keeps the icon always fresh and the extension self-contained while still giving the generator a test, so a change to the drawing that breaks the derivation is caught before a package is cut rather than by inspecting the VSIX. It adds the first test of anything `bundle.js` produces and a way to load that script's code from the test suite, and the test runs only when someone runs `npm test` locally, because CI runs pytest alone. The no-icon-in-a-fresh-checkout and duplicated-parsing costs of the package-time form remain.

alternative.id: Python script run at package time

open-question.alternative: A stdlib-only Python script under the repository's `scripts/`, which can share the banner renderer's parsing, is called by the extension's `vscode:prepublish` step (beside `node scripts/bundle.js`) and writes the icon into the git-ignored `gurita-vscode/bundled/`, where the manifest names it. No icon file is tracked; a pytest test under `tests/` checks the script's output shape from the drawing, so CI tests the generator. It combines an icon that is never stale with a generator tested in CI and written in the language the banner's renderer already uses, so `banner.txt` is parsed by one family of code. Packaging the extension then needs `python3` on the packaging machine, a dependency the Node build step does not have today, and the package-time costs remain: no icon in a fresh checkout until the step runs, and a manifest naming an untracked file.

A Node script under `gurita-vscode/scripts/`, run by hand through an npm script, reads `assets/banner.txt` and writes the icon as a tracked SVG inside `gurita-vscode/` (for example `gurita-vscode/media/`) for the manifest to name. A `node:test` test under `gurita-vscode/src/test/` asserts that the tracked icon equals the script's output, run by `npm test`. The icon is present in every checkout and the VSIX with no build step, and everything about it, script, file, and pin, lives inside the extension's own Node project, independent of the root's Python tooling, as the extension's build already is. The pin never runs in CI, which runs only pytest, so a stale icon is caught only by a maintainer running the extension's tests, and the drawing's parsing is written again in a second language beside `scripts/render_banner.py`.

open-question.question: The mission removes `ideas/vscode_extension.md`, whose section What was checked of VS Code is the repository's only record of the webview-panel facts read from the editor's documentation. Does that record move into another file before the draft is removed, and into which, or does it leave the tree with the draft and stay only in git history?
open-question.alternative: Nothing moves. The What was checked of VS Code section (the custom-editor, publisher, terminal, shell-integration, and webview-panel bullets, dated 2026-11-17 and 2026-11-19) and its Sources list leave the tree with `ideas/vscode_extension.md` and stay only in git history, at the parent of the commit that removes the draft. No file is added or edited for them. It matches the goal's own judgment that the draft is pre-prototype thinking the extension has outgrown. Nothing new has to be kept current, no file gains a section of a different kind, and anyone who needs a fact can read it back with one `git show` of the removed file or check it again against the editor's documentation and the installed `vscode.d.ts`. The repository loses its only readable record of the webview-panel facts just as this mission builds several webview panels at once. Those facts include the serializer rule, the hidden-panel context loss, `createWebviewPanel` making a new panel on every call, and the sources disagreeing about messages to a hidden panel. No missions-tool query serves an `ideas/` file, so a later reader has to know the removed path and the commit to find them, and in practice the facts will be read again from the docs.

Before the draft is removed, the whole section and the Sources entries it cites are moved, as written and with their dates, into `ideas/vscode_extension_follow_up.md` as a section of their own. The webview-panel facts stay on the 2026-11-19 reading and nothing is re-checked. The facts stay in `ideas/`, which is where design research is versioned, inside the one file that already succeeds the draft as the extension's open design record. The follow-up file's publication item already lists the publication facts left unchecked, so the checked publisher and name facts would sit beside the decision they bear on. The follow-up file is a record of what the first version left out, with nothing decided in it. A block of dated documentation readings is a different kind of content, and it would make the file longer without serving that purpose. How the moved section fits that file's references to the draft depends on the axis the follow-up references question owns.

Before the draft is removed, the facts the extension still relies on are moved, with their dates and sources, into `gurita-vscode/README.md` as a section of their own. These are the webview-panel, terminal, and shell-integration bullets. The custom-editor and publisher bullets leave the tree with the draft and stay only in git history. The facts that govern how the code behaves (panels, serializer, hidden context, terminals that survive a reload) sit beside the code and its build instructions. A contributor changing the extension reads that file and it ships with the extension, so the record stays where the work on it happens. The README describes the extension as it stands, and every task in flight in that scope edits it. Dated quotations from the editor's documentation go stale there without notice, and they mix contributor research into a page written for people installing and using the extension. The custom-editor and publisher facts a later publication decision would weigh are lost from the tree.

Before the draft is removed, the whole section and its Sources entries are moved, as written and dated, into a new tracked Markdown file under `gurita-vscode/` that holds only the checked VS Code facts, with its name left to the work. The file is added to `.vscodeignore` so the VSIX does not carry it, and `CLAUDE.md`'s repository layout names it. Later checks, such as this mission's tree-API reading, can be added there. The record keeps everything it holds and gets a home of one kind, next to the code it constrains. It can grow as later missions check further surfaces of the editor, and it shows no unrelated content. It adds a file to keep current and a layout entry to maintain, and it has to stay out of the package by an ignore rule, which is easy to forget. It also keeps alive a body of dated readings that the goal treated as part of what the extension had outgrown.

Before the draft is removed, the whole section and its Sources entries are moved, as written and dated, into a new file under `ideas/` that holds only the checked VS Code facts, with its name left to the work. `CLAUDE.md`'s `ideas/` layout entry is updated to list it in place of the removed draft. The record survives whole, in its own file, in the directory the repository already uses for versioned design research that precedes any mission. Nothing is packaged, and the follow-up record and the README are left untouched. `ideas/` holds drafts that precede missions, so it is a weaker home for standing reference facts than a place beside the code. A later extension mission may not look there, and the file can go stale in the same way the draft did.

Before the draft is removed, the facts that bear on this mission's goal are carried, with their dates, into `## Relevant starting state` of this mission's `requirements.md`. These are the webview-panel and terminal bullets. The rest of the section and its Sources list leave with the draft. When the mission finishes, the carried facts leave the tree with the mission directory, readable afterwards through the missions tool's `show` of the finished mission. The facts reach exactly the deciders who need them now. The alternatives agents, the recommendation pass, `derive-tasks`, and the completion procedure all read that section, and the restore, hidden-window, and read-lifetime questions turn on these facts. Afterwards they stay reachable by a tool query rather than a raw git read, and no permanent file is added. Once the mission finishes, the facts are as hidden from later missions as git history would leave them, and the custom-editor and publisher facts are lost from the tree straight away.

Before the draft is removed, the section is divided by what each part bears on. The publication facts go next to the deferred publication decision that will weigh them, and the runtime facts go next to the extension that depends on them, so nothing still useful leaves the tree. It edits two files of different kinds, so it carries both their costs: a deferred-work record gains checked facts, and a user-facing README gains dated research quotes that go stale without notice. open-question.question: Today's mission pane shows the line `No mission is live.` when no mission is live, and one failure state naming the cause when the read of the live missions fails. Once the missions are listed in a native side-bar tree, how does that view show each of those two states, in which it has no mission row to draw?
open-question.recommendation: One dynamic surface serves both states: the message is drawn above the tree whatever rows the tree holds, so it stays right when the tree lists no mission but still holds other rows, where welcome content would not show, it names the cause in the view as the pane's failure state does today, and it needs no manifest entry, context key, or placeholder row.
open-question.alternative: Both states are drawn through the tree view's own `message` property (`TreeView.message`), with the tree returning no rows. With no mission live the message is today's line `No mission is live.`. When the live read fails it is today's failure line `The live missions could not be read.` followed by the cause as the read gave it. A successful read with missions clears the message. Nothing is added to the manifest, and the view's other contents (its title-bar controls included) stay as they are in every state. One dynamic surface serves both states. It sits in the view itself, carries the cause verbatim exactly as the pane's failure state does today, is set and cleared from the same code path that answers each live read, and needs no manifest entry, context key, or extra command, so a stub of the `vscode` module can cover it by recording one property. The message is one plain-text string rendered above the tree, with no Markdown, link, or button. A long or multi-line cause (a Python traceback or git's message) is shown cramped or cut short in a narrow side bar. Neither state offers an action in the body of the view, so with no mission live a person finds New mission and Define mission only where the sibling question on the side-bar controls places them.

Both states are drawn as tree rows that are not missions, returned by the tree data provider in place of mission rows. With no mission live the provider returns one row labelled `No mission is live.`, with no command. When the live read fails it returns one row labelled with the failure line and an error `ThemeIcon`, the cause carried in the row's tooltip and also as non-clickable child rows, one per line of the cause, so expanding the row shows it whole. Each placeholder row carries its own `contextValue`, so no mission menu or click handler applies to it. Everything stays inside the one tree data provider and the one tree. The cause can be shown in full, line by line, however long it is, and can be inspected or copied from the tooltip. No manifest welcome entry, context key, or second rendering mechanism is needed. A placeholder row looks like any other row, so it reads as something to click or expand. Every piece of code that handles rows (the click that opens a mission's window, row menus, the running marker, and the counts) has to tell placeholder rows from mission rows. Any row layout the sibling question on mission rows settles (for example, whether rows expand) has to be kept from leaking into the placeholders. The view also loses VS Code's own empty-view look.

Both states are drawn as `viewsWelcome` content contributed in the manifest for the view. It shows only while the tree has no rows, and the extension picks which entry shows by setting a context key with `setContext` (for example, none live versus read failed). The no-mission entry reads `No mission is live.`. The failure entry reads `The live missions could not be read.`, but its text is static manifest text and cannot hold the cause. So the cause is written to an output channel the extension contributes, and the failure entry carries a command link or button that reveals that channel. Either entry may also carry command links in Markdown, such as Refresh. This is VS Code's native idiom for an empty view. Its Markdown, links, and buttons can put the next action (refreshing, or starting a mission) right in the body of the view, and the extension keeps no extra rows or message text. The cause is no longer in the view itself: a person has to follow a link to an output channel, unlike today's failure state, which names the cause on the page. The approach adds a manifest entry per state, a context key that must be kept true to every read (so the wrong entry never shows, including before the first read lands), an output channel, and a command, and the editor-stub tests cover none of that content. Any button for New mission or Define mission placed in the welcome entries overlaps the axis the sibling question on the side-bar controls owns.

alternative.id: Welcome when none, message on failure

open-question.alternative: Each state gets the surface that fits its content. With no mission live, the view shows `viewsWelcome` content from the manifest, reading `No mission is live.` and optionally carrying command links. When the live read fails, the tree returns no rows and the extension sets `TreeView.message` to the failure line followed by the cause, and it sets a context key that suppresses the welcome entry while the failure stands, so the welcome entry does not also show. A successful read clears both. The fixed state uses the static, native empty-view surface, which can carry actions. The failing state uses the dynamic surface, which carries the cause verbatim in the view as today. Neither state needs placeholder rows or an output channel. Two mechanisms are coordinated by one context key, and a missed update can leave the welcome text and the failure message showing together, or neither. The failure message is still plain text with no link, and long causes are cramped in a narrow side bar. Any welcome-entry button for New mission or Define mission overlaps the axis the sibling question on the side-bar controls owns.

alternative.id: Welcome when none, row on failure

open-question.alternative: With no mission live, the view shows `viewsWelcome` content from the manifest reading `No mission is live.`, optionally with command links. When the live read fails, the tree returns one placeholder row labelled with the failure line and an error `ThemeIcon`, with the cause in its tooltip and as non-clickable child rows, one per line. Because the tree then has a row, the welcome entry is hidden by VS Code itself and needs no context key. The empty state gets the native, action-capable welcome surface, and the failure state shows the full cause, line by line, inside the view. Since a row hides the welcome content, the two states can never show together and no context key needs to be kept in sync. The failure row is a non-mission row, so every row handler (click, menus, running marker, counts) must tell it apart, and it can look clickable. The two states use two different mechanisms. alternative.id: Blank when none, message on failure

open-question.alternative: With no mission live, the view draws nothing: the tree returns no rows, and the extension contributes no welcome content and sets no message, so the line `No mission is live.` is dropped. When the live read fails, the extension sets `TreeView.message` to the failure line followed by the cause, and clears it on the next successful read. This option has the least code and manifest of all. It keeps only the state that tells a person something has gone wrong, names its cause verbatim in the view, and treats an empty list as needing no words. A blank view cannot be told apart from one whose first read has not landed yet or one that failed to draw, and it drops a line the pane shows today. A first-time user also gets no pointer to starting a mission, which is left entirely to wherever the sibling question on the side-bar controls places New mission and Define mission.

Each step or count that could not be read is replaced, on its own, by one fixed placeholder in its slot, the facts that did read drawn as usual. Each step or count that could not be read is replaced, on its own, by a short text of its cause written in the slot itself, such as `TASKS_TODO.md missing`, `open_questions.xml does not parse`, or `git read failed`, the facts that did read drawn as usual. open-question.question: The banner's SVG draws each character of the drawing as text in a system monospace font, in three colours, on a grid of 10 by 20 pixels per cell. The editor shows an activity-bar icon at 24 by 24 pixels in one fill colour. In what form does the icon script draw the three arms in the icon's SVG, and how much of each arm's detail (its brackets, suckers, and curl) does the icon keep at that size?
open-question.alternative: The icon script derives each arm's outline from the drawing as a filled tapering shape with its curl, in one fill colour, and grades the detail by arm size: the large centre arm keeps its suckers as round holes cut out of the fill, while the two smaller side arms are drawn as plain silhouettes with no holes; brackets survive only as the shapes' edges. Detail is spent only where the pixels can show it: the centre arm carries the sucker motif that identifies the mark, and the side arms stay clean instead of filling with sub-pixel holes that blur into grey. The three arms are no longer drawn by one uniform rule, so the script carries a per-arm detail switch on top of the outline tracing, and the arms differ in kind as well as in size; the rule only makes sense if the three-arm derivation question leaves the side arms clearly smaller than the centre one.

The icon script draws the three arms the way `scripts/render_banner.py` draws the banner: one `text` element per row of the arms' characters, in the same system monospace font stack on the 10 by 20 grid, scaled into the 24 by 24 icon by the SVG's `viewBox`, with every character in one fill colour instead of the three-colour mask. Every bracket, sucker, dash, and curl character of each arm is kept, and no glyph is converted to paths. It carries the banner's own recorded rendering decision (characters drawn as text in a system monospace font, no glyph converted to paths) over to the icon unchanged and can reuse the renderer's row-to-`tspan` logic almost as it stands, so the icon is the banner's drawing in the most literal sense. At 24 by 24 pixels three arms about ten columns wide and ten rows tall give each character well under one pixel of width and under two of height, so the glyphs anti-alias into an indistinct smear whose brackets and suckers cannot be told apart; and since the shape is whatever monospace font the viewer's system supplies to an SVG loaded as an image, the icon's silhouette differs from one machine to the next. How the centre arm is made larger (a scale transform or a different font size) is the three-arm derivation question's to settle.

The icon script draws every character of the three arms as filled path outlines traced from the glyphs of one fixed monospace font, placed on the drawing's cell grid and scaled into the 24 by 24 icon, in one fill colour, keeping every bracket, sucker, dash, and curl character. The icon keeps the banner's typographic look character for character while its shape no longer depends on which font the viewer's system has, so it renders identically everywhere. It needs a font file (tracked in the repository or pulled in as a dependency, with its licence) and a parser for its glyph outlines, which Python's standard library does not provide, so its viability depends on the language the icon script pipeline question settles; and at 24 pixels the outlines smear exactly as the text glyphs do, so the cost buys consistency of a mark that is still illegible in detail.

The icon script maps each character of the drawing to a small vector primitive of its own, drawn in its cell in one fill colour: `o` a dot or ring, `(` and `)` arcs, `/` and `\` diagonal strokes, `-`, `~`, `'`, `,`, `.` and `|` short strokes or ticks, so every bracket, sucker, and curl element of each arm is kept as its own shape, with no font involved. It is font-independent and deterministic like any vector form while still deriving the icon mechanically, character by character, from `assets/banner.txt`, so the icon follows the drawing if the drawing changes and needs no font file. The script must carry a hand-made shape for every character the arms use, a small glyph table that is itself new design; and at under a pixel per cell the many tiny strokes still blur together, so the per-character fidelity is mostly invisible at the size the editor shows.

The icon script reads the drawing as a grid and fills one rectangle for every non-space cell of the three arms, merged into a solid shape per arm, in one fill colour; the brackets, suckers, and curl characters all become filled cells of the same mass, so each arm keeps its overall outline (stem and curl) and none of its internal detail. It is the simplest form to generate and test, a direct and deterministic function of `banner.txt` with no font and no geometry beyond the grid, and a solid silhouette is what a one-colour 24-pixel icon reads best as. The arms come out blocky and stepped rather than as smooth tentacles, the suckers that make them read as octopus arms disappear entirely, and the 10 by 20 cell aspect stretches each step vertically, so the mark may read as three jagged bars rather than arms.

The icon script fills one rectangle for every non-space cell of the three arms in one fill colour except the sucker cells (the `o` characters, slate in the banner's colour mask), which it leaves empty as gaps in the arm; brackets and curl cells are filled, so each arm keeps its outline and its suckers as negative space. It keeps the sucker motif, the one detail that tells an octopus arm from any curved bar, while staying as simple and font-independent as the solid cell silhouette, and it turns the banner's third colour into the only form a one-colour icon can show. A single smooth curved stroke per arm stays crisp and legible at 24 pixels, matches the line weight of the editor's other activity-bar icons, and reads at a glance as three curling tentacles. The script must interpret the ASCII art as geometry (find each row's stem position and turn the curl's characters into a curve), more code with heuristics tuned to this drawing, and the result keeps the drawing's pose but none of its characters, so a change to `banner.txt` may need the heuristics revisited.

The icon script derives each arm's outline from the drawing, its edges taken from the bracket positions on each row and the curl's outer and inner edge, and draws it as a filled tapering shape in one fill colour, with each sucker cut out as a small round hole (an even-odd or masked sub-path); the brackets survive as the shape's edge, the curl as its curled end, and the suckers as holes, for all three arms alike. It is the most recognisable form of an octopus arm a one-colour icon can carry, a smooth filled tentacle with visible suckers, and it uses all three kinds of the drawing's detail rather than discarding any. It needs the most geometry of any option, edges and curl traced from characters plus hole placement, and on the two smaller side arms the holes come out around a pixel or less, so they may blur into the fill and add generation cost for detail only the centre arm can show; how much smaller the side arms are is the three-arm derivation question's to settle.
